newsitem.title: ITALY: Stet's French deal seen as smart move.
newsitem.headline: Stet's French deal seen as smart move.

text.p: Italian state-controlled telecoms holding Stet's entry into France in partnership with conglomerate Bouygues is a smart move for a firm with a haphazard international strategy, analysts said on Friday.
"It's sensible," said Philip Townsend, telecoms analyst with brokers Smith Barney in London.
"Stet isn't tied up in any group yet. Its international policy is scattered. It needs effectively to establish itself in Europe as a powerful force," he said.
Bouygues said late on Thursday that Stet would take a 49 percent stake in a new joint venture called Bouygues-Stet in which the French group would hold 51 percent.
Stet has focused much of its foreign expansion efforts in Latin America but unlike many of its European rivals, had so far failed to hook up with a big international telecoms partner.

It is still involved in long-running talks with U.S. computer giant IBM over a planned global communications deal while an agreement late last year to invest in Russian telecoms venture AO Svyazinvest fell through before completion.
The Italian government has been anxious for the firm to secure a prestigious ally to boost the company's appeal before Stet's planned privatisation, due by March 31 next year.

The new venture, which aims to be a major player in the French telecoms market after it is liberalised in 1998, plans to bid next week for the telephone infrastructure of French state railways group SNCF in partnership with Germany's VEBA.
Stet will also buy into the BDT holding company, which is the 51-percent owner of Bouygues Telecom.
Bouygues said Stet would, during 1996 and 1997, pay 1.71 billion francs ($330 million) to buy new BDT shares. Stet will end up with a 19.6 percent stake in the enlarged BDT.
Analysts said it was still early days to assess the profit potential of the new alliance, but Townsend said Stet had not overpaid. "It's paid up for it, but then you have to," he said.
Stet shares were 0.38 percent firmer at 5,235 lire in early afternoon trade after touching a high of 5,250.
Stet has long hankered after a deal with either Bouygues or Britain's Cable & Wireless Plc, but talks proved tricky.
"We've seen the bear, but haven't yet killed it, so we can't claim the fur yet," Stet managing director Ernesto Pascale said in June, referring to both sets of negotiations.
Pascale paraded his enthusiasm for finally having secured his trophy in a newspaper interview on Friday. "It's a really good day for Stet," he told financial daily Il Sole 24 Ore.
"We're entering the French market, the fifth in the world, and giving life to a Franco-Italian alliance that can go far."

The Bouygues-Stet deal also indirectly gives Stet links with its other former would-be partner, Cable & Wireless, which has a stake in Bouygues Telecom along with VEBA, US West International and banks BNP and Paribas.
"It's a good deal for Stet...It gives Stet a chance to get into joint-ventures, even on the mobile side," said Marco Nascimbeni, head of operations at Milan brokers Carnegie Italia.
Bouygues started France's third mobile telecoms network in May. Stet already controls Telecom Italia Mobile (TIM), Europe's biggest mobile phone group.

Pascale said the Bouygues venture would "make concrete our ambitions to operate across the board internationally with an eye above all on those markets and those businesses, such as those for big users, which are the most profitable".
Stet said last month it planned to spend some four trillion ($2.7 billion) lire on international development in 1997-99. ($1=5.18 francs, $1=1,520 lire)
